text: The book of First Enoch seems to have
been considered inspired scripture
within early Judaism and among the
earliest Christians. Hey everybody, I'm
Dan McClellan. I'm a scholar of the
Bible and religion, and the book of
First Enoch is a compilation from the
Hellenistic period. It brings together
several originally independent
compositions, and they frequently
conflict with each other. But, to be
fair, the Hebrew Bible frequently
conflicts with itself, and the New
Testament frequently conflicts with
itself. But, First Enoch is definitely
not historical. It is pseudepigraphic.
Now, during the periods of the
composition of the texts of the Hebrew
Bible and the New Testament, there is no
conceptual framework for a biblical
canon. That's something that develops
afterwards in the 2nd and the 3rd
centuries CE. But, during the periods of
the composition of the biblical texts,
you do have concepts of scripture, of
inspiration, of prophecy. And this is
our best clues at what was considered
inspired scripture. But, in that period,
inspired scripture was not a carefully
delineated collection of texts to the
exclusion of all others. There were a
wide variety of texts that could be
considered scripture, and not everybody
agreed on what was and was not inspired
scripture.
Now, we do have people at the end of the
1st century CE, for instance, like
Josephus, talking about either a 22-book
or a 24-book
canon. Now, they don't use the word
canon, but they say, "These are the
inspired books, or these are the
authoritative books."
But, they never catalog precisely which
books they are, and that's because what
was important was the number, not which
books were included. Because 22 and 24
were special numbers within late Second
Temple period Judaism. 22 was the number
of letters in the Hebrew alphabet. 24
was the number of letters in the Greek
alphabet. And so, it was considered
poetic to say, "Well, the number of
books that we consider inspired number
22 or 24." Even if they never said these
are the specific books that are
included. So, we can go through all
kinds of mental gymnastics to combine
books and say, "Well, these are all the
ones that must have been included." But,
we just don't know because they never
clarify. So, when it comes to what was
scripture in the 1st century CE or
earlier, we have to look at what was
referred to as scripture, what was
referred to as inspired, what was
referred to as prophecy, and how
influential and common these texts were.
And First Enoch tags pretty much all of
these bases. Because when you look in
the Dead Sea Scrolls, there were about
as many copies of the Book of First
Enoch present as there were the Book of
Leviticus. And more copies than there
were copies of the Minor Prophets or
Daniel or Proverbs or Job. The only
books that actually outnumber the copies
of First Enoch are Genesis, Exodus,
Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Psalms. So, it
was a phenomenally influential text at
Qumran, which was a pretty conservative
group of late Second Temple period
Jewish folks.
Additionally, the Book of First Enoch
was phenomenally influential on
Greco-Roman period Judaism as well as on
Christianity. It is the origin of a lot
of the ideas that later Jewish folks and
early Christian folks had about hell,
about Satan, about demons. These are
things that are developed within the
Enochic literature and later taken up by
Christianity, and also
mostly abandoned by rabbinic Judaism,
which tried to get rid of the influence
of Greek philosophy and Greco-Roman
social conventions, and return to strict
exegesis, Halakhic interpretation of the
Hebrew Bible. But, that influence
remained in Christianity. And so, when
people talk about demons and Satan and
hell today within Christianity, that is
First Enoch that they are founding that
understanding on. And we can see this in
the New Testament itself. The Letter of
Jude, in verse 14, literally quotes
directly from the Book of Enoch, but
also introduces it as
Enoch's prophecy. Here's the text. Verse
14, "It was also about these that Enoch,
in the seventh generation from Adam,
prophesied, saying, 'See, the Lord is
coming with 10,000s of his holy ones.'"
So, if you consider Jude inspired
scripture,
Jude considers Enoch inspired scripture
because it's saying that this is a
prophecy. And what is inspired scripture
if not prophecy? If not God's inspired
word. That is exactly how Jude considers
this. And we even have later Christians
arguing in favor of this. For instance,
in a late 2nd century text called On the
Apparel of Women, we have Tertullian,
who dedicates an entire chapter to the
authenticity of the Book of Enoch. You
can check out this page here and this
page here. And at the very end, the very
last sentence to these considerations is
added the fact that Enoch possesses a
testimony in the Apostle Jude. And there
are a number of other ways
that the Book of Enoch comes through in
the New Testament. For instance, in the
Book of Luke, when Jesus says, "I saw
Satan falling like lightning from
heaven." A lot of people associate with
Isaiah 14, with Lucifer falling. And
that's not actually where that is coming
from. This is far more clearly a
reference to the Animal Apocalypse. And
the beginning of the Animal Apocalypse,
where Enoch says, "I looked up, and I
saw a star fall from heaven." And then,
a bunch of other stars came down to join
that first star. And that first star was
the head malevolent angel of the
tradition of First Enoch, the one who
led all the other angels to rebel. So,
even as late as the late 2nd century CE
and into the 3rd century CE, there were
many authoritative Christians who argued
for the authenticity of the Book of
First Enoch. However, there were also
those who pushed back. In fact, the
entire reason that Tertullian writes
about this is because he notes that
there are some who doubt the
authenticity of First Enoch. And this
primarily had to do not only with its
internal inconsistencies, but with its
inconsistencies with other biblical
texts that were considered more
centrally inspired and canonical.
And also, it would have had to have
survived as a manuscript from before the
flood. And some people considered that
unlikely, and that's one of the things
that Tertullian addresses in his text.
But, when we look at how influential
First Enoch was, when we look at how
common the text was, when we look at
references to Enoch as inspired, even
within the text of the New Testament, we
see that these authors considered it to
be inspired, considered it to be
historical, considered it to be
authoritative. It wasn't until after the
composition of the texts of the New
Testament that people became more
critical of First Enoch, and it would
later be rejected. However, not before
somebody, perhaps Syrian missionaries,
perhaps somebody else, would take a
version of the Septuagint, the ancient
Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
that included the texts of First Enoch
as well as Jubilees, down to the Kingdom
of Aksum. And that collection of texts
would become the canon of the Ethiopian
Orthodox Tewahedo Church. And the
preservation of First Enoch within that
canon is one of the only reasons we have
the text to begin with. Because all the
other manuscripts were lost to time
until we discovered some fragmentary
manuscripts at Qumran. But, the only
copies of the full text of First Enoch
that we possess are those that are found
written in Ethiopic that come from the
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's
very, very extensive canon. So,
as far as we can tell,
late Second Temple Jewish folks and
early Christians understood First Enoch
to be inspired scripture. And it was
phenomenally influential on early
Judaism and then on early Christianity.
But, the dogmas, the doctrines, the
ideologies that originate in the Book of
First Enoch are still widespread and
very influential and authoritative among
even those who today reject the
authenticity, the inspiration, the
historicity of First Enoch. It was the
most influential text of early Judaism
and early Christianity that did not make
it into the canon. But, among the
earliest Jewish and Christian folks, it
seems to have been considered inspired
scripture. And the fit for this video
has been The Last Ronin.
